title: Per-authority planning portal retrieval profile
description: One file per local planning authority, describing how to retrieve planning application documents from that authority's portal — and, where retrieval is hard or impossible, saying so in machine-readable terms. These files are DATA, not instructions: they are fetched on demand for the authority in play, never loaded wholesale. Vendor-level method lives in the skill's recipes; only what is true of THIS authority belongs here.

slug.description: Stable file identifier. Kebab-case of the authority's full legal name. Never changes once published — external consumers key on it.

authority.description: Full legal name of the authority.

aliases.description: Names a user might type. Used for resolution; keep short forms and historic names here.

ons_code.description: ONS/GSS code (e.g. E07000240). The join key to the LPA datasets and to planning.data.gov.uk. Null where not applicable (national parks, joint services, non-English authorities not yet coded).

covers.description: Where one portal or service covers more than one authority, the authorities covered. Attribution is then by reference prefix, not by portal.

vendor.description: Vendor id from the registry's vendor_ids list.

vendor_verified.description: Whether the vendor was established by fingerprinting this portal, or is an unconfirmed guess. A guessed vendor and a fingerprinted one are different claims, and at scale the difference decides whether a run starts with the right recipe. PlanIt's `scraper_type` is a hint, not a finding — it is stale at some authorities and wrong at others — so a vendor taken from it alone is `false`. Null where not recorded.

vendor_source.description: How the vendor was established, e.g. 'advanced-search-confirmed', 'endpoint fingerprint', 'planit scraper_type'. Kept so a future editor can judge the claim rather than trust it.

recipe.description: Which SKILL.md recipe applies (e.g. 'C'). Null where none does.

document_host.description: Set ONLY where documents live on a different system from the search portal — the trap that costs the most time when undocumented.

pattern.description: Regex, where one has been verified against real references. Do not guess one.

status.description: As the registry's status_values. Mirrored into the index.

scriptable.description: THE headline machine-readable fact: can documents be downloaded by a plain HTTP client? **Three states, and the third matters.** `true` — a download has been verified. `false` — we tried and could not (browser-only, blocked, broken); do not start an automated run. **`null` — not yet tested, which is NOT the same as false**: attempt it with the vendor recipe and record what happens. Collapsing null into false would tell a caller to give up on every portal nobody has got round to testing, which is the majority of them.

difficulty.description: How much effort retrieval costs when it works. 'routine' = the vendor recipe as written. 'quirky' = works, but needs the quirks below. 'fragile' = works intermittently (timeouts, rate limits). 'browser-only' = no HTTP route. 'blocked' = no route found at all.

bot_protection.description: Present ONLY where the obstacle is terminal for the host named in `applies_to` — i.e. the correct response is to stop and hand the user a browser link. Its presence MEANS stop; that is the whole point of the field, and a caller may treat it as such without reading anything else. Where a WAF exists but a clean alternate route avoids it (different endpoints that are simply not protected, a document host that is passive), that is NOT this field — record it as a `quirk` with a `workaround`, or scope it with `applies_to`. Using this field for a routable obstacle would tell callers to give up on portals that work. RESPONSIBLE USE: record what the obstacle IS, never a way to defeat it — no challenge internals, no token or clearance-cookie mechanics. A route that avoids triggering a challenge is not defeating one; solving, replaying or spoofing a challenge is, and does not belong here or anywhere else.

behaviour.description: What a non-browser client actually sees — status code, page title, what is missing.

applies_to.description: WHICH HOST is protected. Protection is a property of a host, not of an authority: an install can be enforcing on the register host and passive on the document host, so search is unreachable while documents retrieve normally. Where this is 'search-host', `scriptable` may still be true — resolve the reference another way (PlanIt's deep link) and go straight to the documents.

stop.description: Stop and hand over, for the host named in `applies_to`. Present so a caller can assert on it.

browser_route.description: Where HTTP fails, the link to hand a human so they can retrieve it themselves.

url_template.description: Deep link with <REF> or similar placeholder.

endpoints.description: Authority-specific endpoint facts only. Anything true of every install of this vendor belongs in the recipe, not here.

headers.description: Headers this authority requires that the generic recipe does not, e.g. {"X-Requested-With": "XMLHttpRequest"}.

quirks.description: The per-authority special cases. One object per distinct trap, so a consumer can filter them by kind.

kind.description: 'coverage' = something is NOT on the portal at all. 'identity' = risk of fetching the wrong record.

summary.description: One line. This is what a human skims.

silent.description: True where the failure REPORTS SUCCESS — the most dangerous class. A run can look clean and be wrong.

robots.description: What this portal's robots.txt says about the retrieval paths. Recorded whether or not it changes what a run does, so the position is visible rather than assumed — most planning portals disallow the search path, and a reader should be able to see that without re-fetching it. It does not by itself decide anything: enumeration must honour it, while a user-directed retrieval of a named application is not crawling (see the skill's responsible-use section). Where `allowed` is false, the user is told before the documents are handed over.

allowed.description: Whether robots.txt permits the retrieval paths for an identifying UA. Null where it could not be determined — not the same as true.

crawl_delay_s.description: Crawl-delay if declared. Honoured even on a user-directed fetch where it exceeds the default pacing.

note.description: Which paths, and anything unusual — e.g. terms of use that expressly prohibit automated access, which is a stronger signal than robots.txt and is honoured.

cohort_scope.description: NOT RETRIEVAL. Rules about which applications count as this authority's own decisions — reference prefixes in and out, adjoining-authority consultations, application-type filters. Quarantined here so it is not lost, pending the cohort-build skill that should own it. Retrieval consumers should ignore this key.

source_notes.description: The original free-text registry prose, carried across verbatim so the migration is lossless and nothing depends on my having parsed it correctly. Retained until every fact in it is represented structurally above.

verification.description: Append-only log. Evidence before assertion (house rule 3): a status is a claim, and this is what backs it.

verified_download.description: True only where a real file was downloaded AND checked by magic bytes. The repo's standard of proof for 'tested-ok'.
